lessons.title: The OSI and TCP/IP models
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a seven-layer colored cake, each layer bearing the name of an OSI layer, from the physical layer at the bottom to the application at the top.
objectives: Name the 7 layers of the OSI model and the 4 layers of the TCP/IP model.
Match each layer with its data unit, its devices and its protocols.
Place an attack or a security control at the right layer.

references.title: ISO/IEC 7498-1, Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) basic reference model
IETF RFC 1122, requirements for Internet hosts (TCP/IP layers)

blocks.text: Why layers?

A network is too complex to be thought of as a single block. Layered models split communication into stages: each layer provides a service to the layer above and relies on the one below. For security, it is a map: you know where attacks and protections sit.
From layer 1 to layer 7: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" (Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).
The TCP/IP model

blocks.title: OSI to reason, TCP/IP to operate
blocks.text: The OSI model is a reference model, used to explain and locate problems. The TCP/IP model is the one that networks and the Internet actually follow. In the exam, you will often be asked for the OSI layer of a protocol or a device.
Encapsulation

blocks.title: Each layer adds its header
blocks.alt: Five-step diagram: the application data receives a TCP header and becomes a segment, then an IP header and becomes a packet, then an Ethernet header and trailer and becomes a frame, finally the frame is transmitted as bits over the physical medium.

nodes.label: Bits
nodes.detail: on the cable or the air

blocks.title: Encapsulation and decapsulation
blocks.text: When sending, each layer adds its control information (header) around the data received from the layer above. When receiving, each layer removes its header and passes the rest to the layer above.
Attacks and protections by layer

rows: ARP spoofing, MAC table flooding, VLAN hopping
Cable tapping, radio jamming, open network jack

blocks.text: A classic firewall filters at layers 3 and 4 (addresses and ports). It does not see that an allowed HTTP request contains an SQL injection: a layer 7 control, such as a WAF, is needed. It is a strong argument for defense in depth.

blocks.title: SOC case: three alerts, three layers
blocks.text: Within the same hour, the analyst receives three alerts: a floor switch reports that two different MAC addresses answer for the gateway's IP address (layer 2, possible ARP spoofing); the firewall sees thousands of SYN requests with no follow-up toward the portal (layer 4); the WAF blocks requests containing apostrophes and SQL keywords (layer 7). Placing each alert at its layer lets the analyst alert the right team: local network, infrastructure, then development.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Architect: I place controls at several layers so that a single failure is not enough.
SOC analyst: knowing which layer an alert sits at tells me which logs to look at.
Auditor: I check that network jacks in public areas are disabled or protected by 802.1X.
CISO: the OSI model is a common language between the network, systems and security teams.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Switch = layer 2 (MAC addresses); router = layer 3 (IP addresses); hub = layer 1.
Units: bits (1), frames (2), packets (3), segments or datagrams (4), data (5 to 7).
ARP links layer 3 (IP) and layer 2 (MAC); it is placed in layer 2.
OSI layers 5, 6 and 7 are grouped in the TCP/IP Application layer.
A packet-filtering firewall (3-4) does not see an application attack (7).
OSI: 7 layers (physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application).
TCP/IP: 4 layers (network access, Internet, transport, application).
Encapsulation: data → segment → packet → frame → bits.
Each layer has its attacks and protections: defense in depth.

lessons.title: Protocols, ports and network attacks
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of two computers shaking hands, with three speech bubbles "SYN", "SYN-ACK" and "ACK" between them.
objectives: Compare TCP and UDP and describe the three-way handshake.
Recognize common ports and unencrypted protocols.
Explain the role of ARP, ICMP, DHCP and DNS.
Describe the classic network attacks and their countermeasures.

blocks.text: TCP or UDP?

rows: DNS, VoIP, live video, NTP, SNMP, syslog

blocks.title: The TCP three-way handshake
blocks.alt: Three-step diagram: the client sends SYN to request a connection, the server answers SYN-ACK to accept, the client confirms with ACK; the connection is then established.

blocks.text: Ports to know

rows: Credentials in clear text → SFTP or FTPS
Everything in clear text → replace with SSH
Email between servers; 587 for authenticated submission
Mostly UDP; TCP for large answers and zone transfers
v1 and v2c in clear text → SNMPv3
Windows file sharing, never to be exposed on the Internet
Remote desktop, a frequent target: behind a VPN with MFA

blocks.text: "Well-known" ports: 0 to 1023. A clear-text service almost always has a secure twin: Telnet→SSH, HTTP→HTTPS, LDAP→LDAPS, IMAP→IMAPS.
Service protocols

rows: Find the MAC address that matches an IP address on the local network
ARP spoofing: pretending to be the gateway
Automatically assign IP address, gateway and DNS
Rogue DHCP server that redirects traffic
Translate a name into an IP address
Cache poisoning, exfiltration through DNS queries

blocks.text: Classic network attacks

blocks.title: Four attacks to recognize
blocks.alt: Two-by-two grid. ARP spoofing, layer 2: the attacker announces their own MAC address for the gateway's IP address and intercepts traffic. SYN flood, layer 4: thousands of SYNs without ACK saturate the server. IP spoofing, layer 3: a fake source address to hide the origin. DNS poisoning, layer 7: a fake answer sends users to a fake site.

blocks.title: Countermeasures
items: ARP spoofing and rogue DHCP: dynamic ARP inspection and DHCP snooping on switches.
SYN flood: SYN cookies, rate limiting, the provider's anti-DDoS protection.
IP spoofing: ingress and egress filtering (refuse outbound packets with a source address that is not yours).
DNS poisoning: DNSSEC, up-to-date resolvers, random source ports.

blocks.title: The clear-text protocol
blocks.text: With Telnet, FTP, HTTP or SNMPv1, anyone listening on the network reads the credentials. A traffic analyzer is enough. These protocols must be disabled or replaced by their encrypted version.
Exam questions do not ask you to know 50 ports by heart, but to recognize a clear-text protocol and its secure replacement. Above all, learn the "security note" column.

blocks.title: SOC case: the talkative DNS
blocks.text: The SIEM reports a workstation sending thousands of DNS queries to the same unknown domain, with long, random subdomains. The analyst recognizes a possible DNS tunnel used to exfiltrate data. The analyst isolates the workstation through the EDR, blocks the domain on the internal resolver and checks that no other workstation queries this domain. Workstations are in any case not allowed to query external DNS servers directly: only the internal resolver is.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Network administrator: I disable unused switch ports and enable port security.
SOC analyst: DNS logs are a gold mine for spotting compromised workstations.
Auditor: I look for Telnet, FTP and SNMPv1 in service inventories.
CISO: RDP and SMB exposed on the Internet are classic ransomware entry points.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: TCP handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. A SYN flood leaves half-open connections.
UDP is connectionless: DNS, SNMP, syslog, NTP, VoIP.
DNS = 53 (UDP and TCP); SSH = 22; Telnet = 23; RDP = 3389; LDAPS = 636.
ARP has no authentication: that is what makes spoofing possible.
Egress filtering: prevents your machines from sending packets with a spoofed source address.
TCP reliable and connection-oriented; UDP fast and connectionless.
Ports: recognize clear-text protocols and their replacements.
ARP, ICMP, DHCP, DNS: useful and open to abuse.
Attacks: ARP and IP spoofing, SYN flood, DNS poisoning and tunneling.

lessons.title: Secure protocols
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a green tunnel through a mountain marked "Internet"; an envelope sealed with a padlock travels inside between two buildings.
objectives: Choose the secure protocol that replaces a clear-text protocol.
Tell apart AH and ESP, transport mode and tunnel mode in IPsec.
Explain what TLS, SSH, DNSSEC and encrypted DNS provide.
Protect email: S/MIME, STARTTLS, SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

references.title: IETF RFC 4301 (IPsec architecture) and NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs
IETF RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3), RFC 4033 (DNSSEC), RFC 7858 (DNS over TLS) and RFC 8484 (DNS over HTTPS)

blocks.text: Replacing clear-text protocols

rows: SFTP (inside SSH) or FTPS (FTP inside TLS)
DNSSEC (integrity); DNS over TLS or HTTPS (confidentiality)

blocks.text: TLS and SSH

blocks.title: TLS, Transport Layer Security
blocks.text: Protocol that authenticates the server with a certificate (and sometimes the client), negotiates session keys and encrypts the exchanges. Versions to use: TLS 1.2 and 1.3. SSL and TLS 1.0/1.1 are obsolete.

blocks.title: SSH, Secure Shell
blocks.text: Encrypted remote administration protocol (port 22). Key-based authentication, rather than passwords, is recommended. SSH is also used for file transfer (SFTP, SCP) and tunnels.
IPsec: securing at the IP level

blocks.title: AH or ESP, transport or tunnel?
blocks.alt: Two-by-two grid. AH: authenticates and protects integrity, without encrypting. ESP: encrypts and protects integrity, it is the usual choice. Transport mode: protects the payload, host to host. Tunnel mode: encapsulates the whole packet inside a new packet, used between two gateways for a site-to-site VPN.

blocks.title: To remember about IPsec
items: IKE negotiates the security associations and the keys (UDP 500, and 4500 for NAT traversal).
AH also protects the IP header: it does not support network address translation (NAT).
A site-to-site VPN generally uses ESP in tunnel mode.
IPsec works at layer 3: it protects all applications without modifying them.

blocks.text: "AH Authenticates, ESP Encapsulates (encrypts). The tunnel hides the whole packet, transport only the content."
Securing DNS

blocks.title: DNSSEC does not encrypt
blocks.text: DNSSEC signs DNS answers: the resolver checks that they really come from the domain and have not been modified. It protects against poisoning, but the queries remain readable. For the confidentiality of queries, DNS over TLS (port 853) or over HTTPS is used.
Securing email

rows: Encrypts transport between servers or with the client
Does not protect the stored message
Encrypts and signs the message end to end
Publishes in DNS the servers allowed to send for the domain
Does not check the address displayed to the user
The sending domain signs the message; the recipient verifies with the key published in DNS
Requires SPF or DKIM to align with the visible address and sets the policy (none, quarantine, reject) and the reports
Blocks nothing without SPF or DKIM

blocks.text: SPF, DKIM and DMARC work together against domain-name spoofing in emails. A domain without DMARC in a "reject" policy can easily be imitated for phishing.

blocks.title: SOC case: the supplier's fake invoice
blocks.text: An accountant reports an invoice received from a usual supplier, with new bank details. The analyst examines the headers: SPF fails, no valid DKIM signature, and the supplier's domain has no DMARC policy, which is why the message was delivered. The analyst blocks the sender, searches for the same message in the other mailboxes, warns the supplier and reminds staff of the procedure of checking any change of bank details by phone.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Architect: I prohibit clear-text protocols on the administration network.
Email administrator: I publish SPF, DKIM and a DMARC policy, then move gradually to reject.
Auditor: I check the accepted TLS versions and the absence of Telnet or SNMPv1.
SOC analyst: SPF, DKIM and DMARC results in the headers help me qualify a phishing email.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: AH = integrity and authentication, NO confidentiality; ESP = confidentiality + integrity.
Tunnel mode = whole packet encapsulated (site-to-site VPN); transport mode = payload only.
DNSSEC = integrity and authenticity of answers, not confidentiality.
SFTP runs over SSH; FTPS runs over TLS.
SNMPv3 is the only version that provides authentication and encryption.
Every clear-text protocol has a secure replacement: SSH, HTTPS, LDAPS, SNMPv3, SFTP.
TLS 1.2 and 1.3; SSH with key-based authentication.
IPsec: AH (integrity), ESP (encryption); transport or tunnel; IKE for the keys.
DNSSEC (integrity), encrypted DNS (confidentiality); email: STARTTLS, S/MIME, SPF, DKIM, DMARC.

flashcards.back: Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away".
Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application.
Bits (1), frame (2), packet (3), segment or datagram (4), data (5-7).
Hub = 1, switch = 2, router = 3, WAF = 7.
Each layer adds its header: data → segment → packet → frame → bits.
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
Connectionless, fast: DNS, SNMP, syslog, NTP, VoIP.
22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 53 DNS, 443 HTTPS, 445 SMB, 636 LDAPS, 3389 RDP.
Telnet→SSH, FTP→SFTP/FTPS, HTTP→HTTPS, LDAP→LDAPS, SNMPv1/2c→SNMPv3.
IP → MAC on the local network, with no authentication: spoofing is possible.
SYNs with no ACK: half-open connections. Countermeasure: SYN cookies.
Long, random subdomains: exfiltration or command and control.
Refuse source addresses that are not yours.

Encryption + integrity. The usual choice.
Tunnel: the whole packet (site to site). Transport: the payload (host to host).
Signs the responses: integrity, not confidentiality.
Encrypted DNS: confidentiality of queries (853 for DoT).
Authorized servers / domain signature / alignment and policy.

revisionSheet: # Revision sheet: OSI and TCP/IP models and secure protocols
OSI (1→7): Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away".
TCP/IP: Network Access (OSI 1-2), Internet (3), Transport (4), Application (5-7).
Units: bits, frame, packet, segment/datagram, data. Devices: hub 1, switch 2, router 3, stateful firewall 4, WAF 7.
Encapsulation: each layer adds its header (TCP ports, IP addresses, MAC addresses).
TCP: connection-oriented, SYN / SYN-ACK / ACK. UDP: connectionless (DNS, SNMP, syslog, NTP, VoIP).
Ports: 21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 161 SNMP, 389 LDAP, 636 LDAPS, 445 SMB, 3389 RDP.
ARP (IP→MAC, no authentication), ICMP (diagnostics), DHCP (configuration), DNS (names): all can be abused.
Attacks: ARP spoofing (ARP inspection), rogue DHCP (DHCP snooping), IP spoofing (ingress/egress filtering), SYN flood (SYN cookies), DNS poisoning (DNSSEC), DNS tunnel (DNS logs).
Replace: Telnet→SSH, FTP→SFTP (SSH) or FTPS (TLS), HTTP→HTTPS, LDAP→LDAPS, SNMPv1/2c→SNMPv3, POP3/IMAP→POP3S/IMAPS.
TLS: 1.2 and 1.3 only. SSH: key-based authentication.
IPsec: AH = integrity without encryption (incompatible with NAT); ESP = encryption + integrity; tunnel = whole packet (site to site); transport = payload; IKE = keys.
DNSSEC = integrity and authenticity; DNS over TLS (853) or HTTPS = confidentiality.
Email: STARTTLS (transport), S/MIME or OpenPGP (end to end), SPF (authorized servers), DKIM (signature), DMARC (alignment and policy).
Pairs not to confuse: switch/router; TCP/UDP; AH/ESP; tunnel/transport; DNSSEC/DoH; SFTP/FTPS; STARTTLS/S/MIME.

questions.prompt: How many layers does the OSI model have?
questions.explanation: Physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application: 7 layers.

whyNot.0: The OSI model does not have 9 layers.
whyNot.1: Some textbooks use a hybrid 5-layer model, but OSI has 7.

questions.prompt: At which OSI layer does a classic switch mainly operate?
questions.explanation: The switch forwards frames based on MAC addresses: layer 2.

whyNot.0: Layer 3 is the router's layer (IP addresses).
whyNot.1: Layer 7 is the layer of applications and WAFs.
whyNot.3: Layer 1 is the layer of hubs and cables.

questions.prompt: What is the data unit of layer 3 called?
questions.explanation: Layer 3 = packet; layer 2 = frame; layer 4 = segment; layer 1 = bit.

whyNot.1: The segment belongs to layer 4.

questions.prompt: In the TCP/IP model, which OSI layers does the Application layer combine?
questions.explanation: The OSI session, presentation and application layers are merged into the TCP/IP Application layer.

whyNot.2: Layers 1 and 2 form the Network Access layer.
whyNot.3: Layers 3 and 4 correspond to Internet and Transport.

questions.prompt: A packet-filtering firewall allows port 443. An HTTPS request contains a SQL injection. Why doesn't the firewall block it?
choices: Because SQL injection acts on layer 1 and slips under the filtering
Because it works at layers 3 and 4 and does not analyze application content
Because port 443 is always safe and encrypted end to end
Because packet-filtering firewalls only inspect UDP traffic
questions.explanation: Injection is a layer 7 attack: it takes an application-level control such as a WAF, which inspects the content after decryption.

whyNot.0: SQL injection is an application attack.
whyNot.2: A port guarantees nothing about the content.
whyNot.3: Firewalls also filter TCP.

questions.prompt: What is encapsulation?
choices: File compression by the presentation layer
Removing IP addresses to hide the sender
Encrypting all the data before it is sent
Each layer adding its own header around the data
questions.explanation: When sending, each layer adds its control information; when receiving, it removes it.

whyNot.1: On the contrary, layer 3 adds the IP addresses.

questions.prompt: Match correctly: which attacks belong to layer 2? (2 answers)
questions.explanation: ARP and MAC addresses belong to the data link layer.

whyNot.1: A SYN flood targets layer 4 (TCP).
whyNot.3: SQL injection is a layer 7 attack.

questions.prompt: Which device makes its forwarding decisions based on IP addresses?
questions.explanation: The router connects different networks at layer 3, based on IP addresses.

whyNot.1: The hub repeats the bits on all ports (layer 1).

questions.prompt: Which measure primarily protects the physical layer?
choices: A web application firewall (WAF) at the front end
Access control to the premises and the network outlets
questions.explanation: Layer 1 is protected by physical measures: access to the premises, cables, outlets.

whyNot.1: TLS acts above the transport layer.

questions.prompt: Which functions are traditionally associated with layer 6 (presentation) of the OSI model? (2 answers)
questions.explanation: The presentation layer handles how data is represented: encoding, compression, encryption.

whyNot.1: Routing belongs to layer 3.

questions.prompt: What is the order of the TCP handshake?
questions.explanation: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the client confirms with ACK.

whyNot.1: The order is reversed.
whyNot.2: FIN is used to close a connection.

questions.prompt: Which protocol mainly uses UDP?
questions.explanation: Ordinary DNS queries use UDP 53; TCP 53 is used for large responses and zone transfers.

whyNot.2: HTTPS uses TCP 443 (and QUIC over UDP for HTTP/3, but the classic case is still TCP).
whyNot.3: SSH uses TCP 22.

questions.prompt: Which port does SSH use by default?
questions.explanation: SSH listens on TCP port 22.

whyNot.1: 21 is the FTP command port.

questions.prompt: Which of these protocols sends credentials in cleartext?
questions.explanation: Telnet encrypts nothing: a simple traffic analyzer reveals the credentials.

whyNot.3: SSH encrypts the session.

questions.prompt: Why is ARP spoofing possible?
choices: Because ARP accepts replies without authenticating them
Because ARP only works on the Internet, outside the local network
Because ARP encrypts frames poorly with a key that is too short
Because ARP uses port 443, which is open everywhere
questions.explanation: ARP trusts the replies it receives; an attacker announces their MAC address for the gateway's IP and intercepts the traffic.

whyNot.1: ARP works on the local network.
whyNot.3: ARP does not use a TCP or UDP port.

questions.prompt: What characterizes a SYN flood?
choices: Spoofed DNS requests sent to a resolver
A fake ARP announcement for the gateway's address
Thousands of SYNs with no final ACK, which overwhelm the server
A password guessed by successive attempts
questions.explanation: The server keeps every pending request in memory; it becomes saturated and can no longer accept real clients.

whyNot.1: That is ARP spoofing.
whyNot.3: That is a brute-force or dictionary attack.

questions.prompt: Which measures protect a local network against ARP spoofing and rogue DHCP servers? (2 answers)
choices: Dynamic ARP inspection on the switches
questions.explanation: These switch features only accept ARP and DHCP replies from legitimate sources.

questions.prompt: What is egress filtering used for against IP spoofing?
choices: Blocking outbound packets with a foreign source address
Automatically encrypting all traffic going out to the Internet
Blocking all inbound connections from the Internet to the internal network
Speeding up routing by dropping duplicate packets
questions.explanation: Refusing foreign source addresses on the way out prevents your network from being used for spoofed attacks.

whyNot.1: Filtering encrypts nothing.
whyNot.2: That would be ingress filtering, and far too broad.
whyNot.3: That is not its purpose.

questions.prompt: A workstation sends thousands of DNS queries with long random subdomains to the same unknown domain. What should be suspected?
choices: A speed test of the Internet connection
A printer fault that resends its requests in a loop
A DNS tunnel used to exfiltrate data or control the workstation
questions.explanation: Long, random subdomains can encode data: it is a classic sign of a DNS tunnel.

whyNot.0: A speed test does not involve thousands of DNS queries.
whyNot.1: A printer does not produce this traffic.
whyNot.3: An update does not have this profile.

questions.prompt: Which service must never be exposed directly to the Internet?
choices: An internal DNS resolver reachable only internally
questions.explanation: Exposed SMB is a classic entry point for worms and ransomware.

whyNot.0: An inbound mail server must be reachable, with its protections.
whyNot.1: A public site is meant to be exposed, over HTTPS.
whyNot.3: An internal resolver is precisely not exposed.

questions.prompt: What should replace Telnet for administering a server?
questions.explanation: SSH provides an encrypted, authenticated administration channel.

whyNot.1: FTP transfers files in cleartext.

questions.prompt: Which component of IPsec provides confidentiality?
questions.explanation: ESP encrypts the payload (and protects its integrity); AH only provides integrity and authentication.

whyNot.0: IKE negotiates the keys but does not encrypt the traffic itself.
whyNot.1: AH does not encrypt.
whyNot.3: ICMP is a diagnostic protocol.

questions.prompt: Which IPsec mode is generally used for a site-to-site VPN between two gateways?
questions.explanation: In tunnel mode, the original packet is fully encapsulated in a new packet between the gateways.

whyNot.1: This mode does not exist in IPsec.
whyNot.2: This mode does not exist in IPsec.
whyNot.3: Transport mode protects the payload from host to host.

questions.prompt: Why is AH incompatible with network address translation (NAT)?
choices: Because AH encrypts the IP address, which NAT can no longer read
Because AH protects the integrity of part of the IP header, which NAT modifies
Because AH only works in IPv6, where NAT does not exist
Because AH uses port 445, which NAT devices block
questions.explanation: NAT changes the IP address; AH's integrity check then fails.

whyNot.2: AH exists in both IPv4 and IPv6.
whyNot.3: AH does not use a port.

questions.prompt: What does DNSSEC provide?
choices: Compression of domain names in responses
Integrity and authenticity of DNS responses through signatures
Confidentiality of DNS queries through encryption
questions.explanation: DNSSEC signs the responses; it protects against poisoning but does not encrypt.

whyNot.3: Confidentiality comes from DNS over TLS or HTTPS.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms help prevent a company's domain name from being spoofed in emails? (2 answers)
questions.explanation: DKIM signs the domain's messages; DMARC enforces alignment and the policy to apply on failure (with SPF).

whyNot.1: Telnet has nothing to do with secure email.
whyNot.3: POP3 is used to retrieve mail, in cleartext.

questions.prompt: What does an SPF record publish?
choices: The password of the domain's mailboxes
The list of servers allowed to send for the domain
The private key of the domain's mail server
questions.explanation: SPF, published in DNS, lists the authorized sending sources.

whyNot.1: Retention falls under an internal policy.
whyNot.3: A private key is never published.

questions.prompt: Which protocol is SFTP built on?
questions.explanation: SFTP runs inside an SSH channel; FTPS, on the other hand, adds TLS to FTP.

whyNot.1: FTPS is built on TLS, not SFTP.
whyNot.3: Telnet is in cleartext.

questions.prompt: Which configurations are recommended today? (2 answers)
questions.explanation: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 and SNMPv3 are the secure versions; SSL and TLS 1.0/1.1 are obsolete.

whyNot.1: SSL 3.0 is broken (POODLE attack).
whyNot.3: TLS 1.0 is obsolete and withdrawn.

questions.prompt: A message is encrypted with STARTTLS between the servers. Is it protected once stored in the recipient's mailbox?
choices: No, because STARTTLS disables the DKIM signature of the stored message
Yes, STARTTLS encrypts the message end to end, all the way into the mailbox
No, STARTTLS only protects the transport, not the stored message
Yes, but only if the message contains an encrypted attachment
questions.explanation: STARTTLS encrypts the connection; the message is in cleartext on each server. S/MIME or OpenPGP encrypt the content end to end.

whyNot.1: STARTTLS protects the connection, not the stored content.
whyNot.3: Having an attachment changes nothing.
